claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is a refractory high-entropy or refractory concentrated alloy.
The as-cast HfNbTaTiZr material is a single-phase solid solution.
The as-cast HfNbTaTiZr state has significant residual stresses and a high dislocation density.
Slight annealing will relieve residual stresses and lower the defect or dislocation density relative to the as-cast state.
Residual stress and dislocation density changes are reflected by changes in lattice parameter measurable by high-energy diffraction.
Lattice parameter and dislocation-density changes mediate the elastic modulus, yield behavior, and thermal expansion of the alloy.
Higher residual stresses and a more defective dislocation network enhance lattice vibrational amplitudes and lattice softening at 1000–1600°C.
Higher residual stresses and dislocation density promote earlier activation of dislocation slip or recovery at elevated temperatures.
Enhanced lattice softening and accelerated dislocation activity reduce the effective elastic modulus.
Enhanced lattice softening and accelerated dislocation activity reduce yield strength.
Enhanced lattice vibrational softening increases thermal expansion.
Under identical elevated-temperature testing, the as-cast alloy will have a statistically significantly lower elastic modulus than the annealed baseline.
Under identical elevated-temperature testing, the as-cast alloy will have a statistically significantly lower yield strength than the annealed baseline.
Under identical elevated-temperature testing, the as-cast alloy will have a higher thermal expansion coefficient than the annealed baseline.
The proposed trends should hold from approximately 1000°C to 1600°C under controlled strain-rate conditions.
The comparison should use as-cast and slightly annealed HfNbTaTiZr samples tested with identical strain rates and temperature ramps.
A lack of statistically significant differences, or trends opposite to those predicted, would falsify the hypothesis.
